doc.title: Vince DiMartino interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, January 8, 2025

title: Writing for Viper, Kentucky and the 'Heyden' jury
summary: He wrote his manual for a trumpeter in Viper, Kentucky, and tells of a freshman mispronouncing Haydn at a jury.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Becoming a teacher: jazz in schools and conservatories

blocks.x: Well thank you. You know the reason is because I think if your mission is related to people and you care about what they’re doing, that’s the vibe they get. Because I always wonder, I say I’m just doing what I’m supposed to do I thought. I thought everybody did that. Because I can say that’s how clueless I really was and still am sometimes. And the thing with the syllabus too that I wrote and all of that, I said, of course with my background, and I tell people this I said, “Do you know where Viper, Kentucky is?” And they go, “No.” I said, “Well they have a stoplight there and there’s a gas station. And I want a trumpet player who lives in Viper, Kentucky and has no help, to be able to learn to play trumpet by the words that I’ve written in this book. It has to be written in human language. Not some esoteric music trumpet guru type of stuff. Otherwise who understands that? That’s not their vernacular. You know? So for me that was always the most important thing. And so when they came to school, even if, you know, one of my students said something I’ll never forget. He was a freshman, okay? And he was playing his jury, you know his jury exam. Every semester that you take applied lessons you have to play for the class faculty and then they give you comments and they try to help you and, you know, that’s great. So and what I used to do, especially with the freshmen that I knew were nervous playing their first, you know, jury. And they’re standing up on a stage and people are looking at them. They’ve never played a recital. Well usually they’ve

played one because everybody gets on stage once at a big recital that everybody plays on, and plays all or part of a movement of a piece and only with the trumpet players there as their audience. So anyway they’ve been on stage. But in the meantime they haven’t been in this situation where they’re getting graded for it, you know, and stuff. So I get off stage and I said, “Well, John, what are you going to play?” And he goes, “I’m going to play that there Heyden song.” And I realized where I was, you know what I mean? He never said that in, because I never asked him that question you know. And I felt bad because you know the faculty, one of them laughed you know what I mean? And I just — oh gosh this is awful. I said, this isn’t going to happen to anybody. I have to teach people, you know, how to — and I never said, “Haydn song” in lessons. You know but every time a student mispronounced a word, I said, “Oh no, that’s not Heyden” it’s Haydn. I said, “I used to say Heyden.” But you’re going to say Haydn.
Yeah. Make them feel okay about it, yeah.
